solution:
By the first law of thermodynamics, \(\Delta U = q + \text{w}\), with the sign convention that \(q\) is positive when heat is absorbed BY the system and \(\text{w}\) is positive when work is done ON the system.
Heat absorbed by the system: \(q = +701\,\text{J}\).
Work is done BY the system, so the work done on the system is negative: \(\text{w} = -394\,\text{J}\).
\(\Delta U = 701\,\text{J} + (-394\,\text{J})\)
Change in internal energy \(= +307\,\text{J}\) (the internal energy of the system increases by \(307\,\text{J}\)).

[Textbook error — THE QUESTION CONTRADICTS ITSELF, and which reading you take changes the answer. The prose introduces the reactant as \(\text{NH}_2\text{CN}(s)\) while the equation printed directly beneath it writes \(\text{NH}_2\text{CN}(g)\). The two readings give different \(\Delta n_g\) and therefore different answers, and BOTH are internally consistent: as a SOLID, \(\Delta n_g = 2 - 1.5 = +0.5\) and \(\Delta H = -741.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\); as a GAS, \(\Delta n_g = 2 - 2.5 = -0.5\) and \(\Delta H = -743.9\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). The answer below takes the SOLID, for two reasons: it is what the question's own prose states, and cyanamide melts near \(44\,^\circ\text{C}\) so it is a solid at the stated \(298\,\text{K}\) — a bomb calorimeter is loaded with the solid. THE PRINTED ANSWER KEY TAKES THE GAS: it prints \(-743.939\,\text{kJ}\), which is reproduced to all six figures by \(-742.7 - 0.5(8.314\times10^{-3})(298)\). Both values are named here because an examiner following the book's key will expect \(-743.9\), and a student who answered \(-741.5\) from the printed prose is not wrong.] A bomb calorimeter operates at constant volume, so the measured heat is \(\Delta U\). The enthalpy change is obtained from
\(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g \text{R}T\)
where \(\Delta n_g\) is (moles of gaseous products) \(-\) (moles of gaseous reactants).
For \(\text{NH}_2\text{CN}(s) + \dfrac{3}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{N}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\):
gaseous products \(= 1 + 1 = 2\,\text{mol}\); gaseous reactants \(= \dfrac{3}{2}\,\text{mol}\) (the cyanamide is a solid and the water is a liquid).
\(\Delta n_g = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5\)
\(\Delta H = -742.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} + (0.5)(8.314 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1})(298\,\text{K})\)
\(= -742.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1} + 1.24\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta H = -741.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
_note: The stem names cyanamide as \(\text{NH}_2\text{CN}(s)\) in prose but writes \(\text{NH}_2\text{CN}(g)\) in the printed equation. The prose state (solid) is used, giving \(\Delta n_g = +0.5\). On the gaseous reading \(\Delta n_g = -0.5\) and \(\Delta H = -743.9\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

solution:
Heat required at constant pressure is \(q = n\,C_m\,\Delta T\), where \(C_m\) is the molar heat capacity.
Molar mass of aluminium \(= 27\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), so
\(n = \dfrac{60.0\,\text{g}}{27\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 2.22\,\text{mol}\)
A temperature rise from \(35\,^\circ\text{C}\) to \(55\,^\circ\text{C}\) is \(\Delta T = 20\,^\circ\text{C} = 20\,\text{K}\) (a temperature DIFFERENCE is the same number in \(^\circ\text{C}\) and in \(\text{K}\)).
\(q = (2.22\,\text{mol})(24\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1})(20\,\text{K}) = 1066.7\,\text{J}\)
Heat required \(= 1.07\,\text{kJ}\).

Enthalpy is a state function, so the overall change is the sum of the changes along any convenient path. Take three steps:
Step 1 — cool the liquid from \(10.0\,^\circ\text{C}\) to \(0\,^\circ\text{C}\):
\(\Delta H_1 = n\,C_p[\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)]\,\Delta T = (1.0)(75.3\,\text{J K}^{-1})(-10.0\,\text{K}) = -753\,\text{J} = -0.753\,\text{kJ}\)
Step 2 — freeze at \(0\,^\circ\text{C}\). Freezing is the reverse of fusion, so its enthalpy is \(-\Delta_{fus}H\):
\(\Delta H_2 = -6.03\,\text{kJ}\)
Step 3 — cool the ice from \(0\,^\circ\text{C}\) to \(-10.0\,^\circ\text{C}\):
\(\Delta H_3 = n\,C_p[\text{H}_2\text{O}(s)]\,\Delta T = (1.0)(36.8\,\text{J K}^{-1})(-10.0\,\text{K}) = -368\,\text{J} = -0.368\,\text{kJ}\)
Total:
\(\Delta H = -0.753 - 6.03 - 0.368\)
\(\Delta H = -7.15\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) (heat is released, as expected for freezing and cooling).

The enthalpy of combustion is quoted per mole of carbon burnt, and one mole of carbon gives one mole of \(\text{CO}_2\), so the heat released is proportional to the moles of \(\text{CO}_2\) formed.
Molar mass of \(\text{CO}_2 = 12 + 2(16) = 44\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\)
\(n(\text{CO}_2) = \dfrac{35.2\,\text{g}}{44\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.8\,\text{mol}\)
Heat released \(= n \times |\Delta_c H| = (0.8\,\text{mol})(393.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}) = 314.8\,\text{kJ}\)
Heat released \(= 314.8\,\text{kJ}\) (equivalently \(\Delta H = -314.8\,\text{kJ}\)).

Using \(\Delta_r H = \sum \Delta_f H(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_f H(\text{reactants})\), each term weighted by its stoichiometric coefficient.
For \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) + 3\text{CO}(g) \rightarrow \text{N}_2\text{O}(g) + 3\text{CO}_2(g)\):
Products: \(\Delta_f H(\text{N}_2\text{O}) + 3\,\Delta_f H(\text{CO}_2) = 81 + 3(-393) = 81 - 1179 = -1098\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Reactants: \(\Delta_f H(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4) + 3\,\Delta_f H(\text{CO}) = 9.7 + 3(-110) = 9.7 - 330 = -320.3\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta_r H = -1098 - (-320.3)\)
\(\Delta_r H = -777.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

The standard enthalpy of formation is defined for the formation of exactly ONE mole of the compound from its elements in their reference states.
The reaction given forms 2 mol of \(\text{NH}_3\):
\(\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3(g)\); \(\Delta_r H^{\ominus} = -92.4\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Halving the equation halves the enthalpy change:
\(\dfrac{1}{2}\text{N}_2(g) + \dfrac{3}{2}\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{NH}_3(g)\)
\(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{NH}_3, g) = \dfrac{-92.4}{2}\)
\(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{NH}_3, g) = -46.2\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

The target is the formation reaction of methanol:
\(\text{C}(\text{graphite}) + 2\text{H}_2(g) + \dfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(l)\)
By Hess's law of constant heat summation, combine the given equations so that they add to the target. Label them
(1) \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}(l) + \dfrac{3}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\); \(-726\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(2) \(\text{C}(\text{graphite}) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g)\); \(-393\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(3) \(\text{H}_2(g) + \dfrac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\); \(-286\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Target \(= (2) + 2 \times (3) - (1)\), so
\(\Delta_f H^{\ominus} = (-393) + 2(-286) - (-726)\)
\(= -393 - 572 + 726\)
\(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}, l) = -239\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Build the process \(\text{CCl}_4(g) \rightarrow \text{C}(g) + 4\text{Cl}(g)\) out of the given steps (Hess's law):
(i) Condense the vapour, the reverse of vaporisation: \(\text{CCl}_4(g) \rightarrow \text{CCl}_4(l)\); \(-30.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(ii) Decompose the liquid into its elements, the reverse of formation: \(\text{CCl}_4(l) \rightarrow \text{C}(\text{graphite}) + 2\text{Cl}_2(g)\); \(+135.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(iii) Atomise the carbon: \(\text{C}(\text{graphite}) \rightarrow \text{C}(g)\); \(+715.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
(iv) Atomise both moles of chlorine: \(2\text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 4\text{Cl}(g)\); \(2 \times 242 = +484\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Adding:
\(\Delta H = -30.5 + 135.5 + 715.0 + 484 = 1304.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
This breaks four equivalent \(\text{C}-\text{Cl}\) bonds, so the mean bond enthalpy is
\(\Delta_{\text{C}-\text{Cl}}H = \dfrac{1304.0}{4} = 326.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
Enthalpy change for the process \(= 1304.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\); mean \(\text{C}-\text{Cl}\) bond enthalpy \(= 326.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

An isolated system exchanges neither matter nor energy with its surroundings, so \(q = 0\) and \(\text{w} = 0\), which is why \(\Delta U = 0\). The internal energy therefore tells us nothing about the direction of change; the criterion of spontaneity for an isolated system is the entropy.
For any spontaneous (irreversible) change inside an isolated system \(\Delta S > 0\); at equilibrium \(\Delta S = 0\). Nothing in the system can make \(\Delta S\) negative, since \(\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys}\) here (the surroundings are unaffected) and \(\Delta S_{total}\) cannot decrease.
For example, an ideal gas expanding freely into a vacuum has \(\Delta U = 0\) yet becomes more disordered, so its entropy rises.
\(\Delta S > 0\) for a spontaneous change (and \(\Delta S = 0\) only if the system is already at equilibrium).

A reaction is spontaneous when the Gibbs energy change is negative:
\(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0\)
Both \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) are positive here, so the reaction can only become spontaneous by making the \(T\Delta S\) term large enough:
\(T\Delta S > \Delta H\)
\(T > \dfrac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}\)
Both quantities are already in \(\text{kJ}\), so no conversion is needed:
\(T > \dfrac{400\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}}{0.2\,\text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}} = 2000\,\text{K}\)
The reaction becomes spontaneous above \(T = 2000\,\text{K}\) (at exactly \(2000\,\text{K}\), \(\Delta G = 0\) and the system is at equilibrium).

\(2\text{Cl}(g) \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2(g)\) is a bond-FORMING process: two chlorine atoms combine to make one \(\text{Cl}-\text{Cl}\) bond. Energy is released when a bond is formed, so the process is exothermic.
\(\Delta H\) is NEGATIVE. (It is the negative of the bond dissociation enthalpy of \(\text{Cl}_2\), about \(-242\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).)
Two moles of gaseous atoms are converted into one mole of gaseous molecules, so the number of gaseous particles falls and the system becomes more ordered.
\(\Delta S\) is NEGATIVE.

\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus} - T\Delta S^{\ominus}\), so the internal energy change must first be converted to an enthalpy change using
\(\Delta H^{\ominus} = \Delta U^{\ominus} + \Delta n_g \text{R}T\)
For \(2\text{A}(g) + \text{B}(g) \rightarrow 2\text{D}(g)\): \(\Delta n_g = 2 - (2 + 1) = -1\).
Taking \(T = 298\,\text{K}\) (standard conditions):
\(\Delta H^{\ominus} = -10.5\,\text{kJ} + (-1)(8.314 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1})(298\,\text{K})\)
\(= -10.5 - 2.478 = -12.98\,\text{kJ}\)
Now
\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = -12.98\,\text{kJ} - (298\,\text{K})(-44.1 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{kJ K}^{-1})\)
\(= -12.98 + 13.14\)
\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = +0.16\,\text{kJ}\)
Since \(\Delta G^{\ominus}\) is positive, the reaction is NOT spontaneous under standard conditions.

The standard Gibbs energy change is related to the equilibrium constant by
\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = -\text{R}T \ln K = -2.303\,\text{R}T \log K\)
With \(K = 10\), \(\log K = 1\):
\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = -2.303 \times (8.314\,\text{JK}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}) \times (300\,\text{K}) \times 1\)
\(= -5744\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)
\(\Delta G^{\ominus} = -5.74\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
The negative value is consistent with \(K > 1\), i.e. products favoured at equilibrium.

The first equation is the formation reaction of \(\text{NO}(g)\) from its elements in their reference states, so \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{NO}, g) = +90\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).
A POSITIVE enthalpy of formation means \(\text{NO}\) lies higher in enthalpy than the elements from which it is made: energy has to be supplied to form it, and it would release energy on decomposing back to \(\text{N}_2\) and \(\text{O}_2\). \(\text{NO}(g)\) is therefore thermodynamically UNSTABLE with respect to its elements.
The second equation shows that \(\text{NO}\) is further oxidised to \(\text{NO}_2\) with \(\Delta_r H^{\ominus} = -74\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), an exothermic change. So \(\text{NO}\) is also unstable with respect to \(\text{NO}_2\) in the presence of oxygen, and it will tend to be converted to \(\text{NO}_2\).
Adding the two equations gives \(\dfrac{1}{2}\text{N}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{NO}_2(g)\); \(\Delta_f H^{\ominus}(\text{NO}_2) = 90 - 74 = +16\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). \(\text{NO}_2\) is also endothermic with respect to the elements, but far less so than \(\text{NO}\), so it is the more stable of the two oxides.
Conclusion: \(\text{NO}(g)\) is thermodynamically unstable — both with respect to its elements and with respect to oxidation to \(\text{NO}_2\).
_note: Strictly, stability is decided by \(\Delta G\) rather than \(\Delta H\); the question supplies only enthalpy data, so the answer argues from the enthalpies as intended by the chapter.

solution:
The heat lost by the system is gained by the surroundings, so at constant pressure
\(\Delta S_{surr} = \dfrac{q_{surr}}{T} = \dfrac{-\Delta_f H^{\ominus}}{T}\)
Formation of \(1.00\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\) releases \(286\,\text{kJ}\), so the surroundings ABSORB \(q_{surr} = +286\,\text{kJ} = +286000\,\text{J}\).
Standard conditions give \(T = 298\,\text{K}\):
\(\Delta S_{surr} = \dfrac{286000\,\text{J}}{298\,\text{K}}\)
\(\Delta S_{surr} = +959.7\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\)
The entropy of the surroundings increases, which is why this strongly exothermic reaction is spontaneous even though the system itself becomes more ordered.
